Catalysis. Catalysis is the acceleration of a chemical reaction by a substance called a catalyst, which is not permanently consumed. Catalysts work by lowering the activation energy—the energy barrier that must be surmounted for reactants to transform into products—allowing reactions to reach equilibrium far more rapidly. Catalysis governs industrial chemistry, all biological processes, and environmental phenomena. Understanding catalysis is essential across chemistry, biochemistry, materials science, and environmental science.

A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with lower activation energy, enabling reactants to transform into products more rapidly without changing the inherent thermodynamics. Catalysts are regenerated unchanged at the end of the reaction. They are not consumed stoichiometrically and can be reused indefinitely until poisoned or deactivated.

The catalyst does not change the Gibbs free energy or equilibrium constant of the reaction. It only accelerates the approach to equilibrium and does not favor products or reactants thermodynamically. The transition state is the highest-energy configuration along the reaction pathway. Catalysts stabilize this state via direct binding, reducing the energy difference between reactants and transition state.

Homogeneous catalysis occurs when the catalyst is dissolved in the same phase as reactants, such as in acid-catalyzed esterification in aqueous solution using sulfuric acid. Heterogeneous catalysis occurs when the catalyst exists in a different phase—commonly a solid catalyst on which gas or liquid reactants adsorb and react, such as platinum in automotive catalytic converters or iron in the Haber-Bosch ammonia synthesis. Enzymatic catalysis uses biological catalysts, usually proteins, to accelerate metabolic reactions with extraordinary specificity, achieving rate accelerations of ten to the sixth through ten to the seventeenth times.

The active site of an enzyme is the region where substrate molecules bind and catalysis occurs. It uses non-covalent interactions like hydrogen bonds, van der Waals forces, and electrostatic interactions to stabilize the transition state and lower activation energy. Enzymes recognize and bind only specific substrates, allowing cells to control metabolism with precision.

In competitive inhibition, an inhibitor competes with substrate for the active site and can be overcome by increasing substrate concentration. Non-competitive inhibition occurs when an inhibitor binds elsewhere at an allosteric site and impairs catalysis regardless of substrate concentration, often used for metabolic regulation.
